messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Network Engineer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Known People: Related people, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Moana is a 33-year-old network engineer who came to treatment nearly two years after her young son was hospitalized with a sudden, life-threatening illness. At the time, she had already been under strain from her divorce, and when her son deteriorated she spent days in the pediatric intensive care unit sleeping upright in a chair, listening to monitors and waiting for staff to rush in. What has stayed with her most sharply is not a single medical detail so much as the atmosphere of emergency around him: clipped disagreements between adults about what should happen next, relatives arriving with frightened faces, and the repeated moments when he had to be taken for another examination or procedure while she stood aside feeling useless. She remembers how every argument near his bed seemed to signal that something was about to go terribly wrong, and how every familiar face coming down the hall carried the possibility of bad news.

In the months after he recovered, Moana found that scenes in ordinary life could hit her with the same sense of imminent danger. At work, if two coworkers in the operations room started arguing over an outage, her body reacted before she had time to think; her chest tightened, her hands went cold, and she felt a jolt of alarm as if she were back outside her son’s hospital room waiting for someone to tell her he might not make it. It was similar when people connected to that period contacted her or appeared unexpectedly—certain relatives, her ex-husband, even other parents who had been involved then. Seeing known people linked in her mind to the illness brought an immediate wave of tension and she became physically agitated, bracing for catastrophe. Medical settings were especially potent. A routine checkup for herself, or accompanying her son to any follow-up procedure, could leave her sweating, shaky, and unable to settle for hours. These reminders did not just upset her; they made the world feel dangerous again, and she became intensely watchful even after the moment had passed.

That sense of danger no longer stays confined to obvious reminders. Moana describes feeling on guard in her own apartment, as if bad news could arrive through the door at any moment. If someone moves suddenly beside her—her son darting into the kitchen, a colleague stepping quickly into her cubicle, a stranger shifting in the waiting room—she startles hard, heart racing, already preparing herself for something awful before she can orient to what is happening. Living in this keyed-up state has made the range of things that set her off feel broader and more immediate. Because she is already scanning for signs of trouble, an argument across the office floor catches her instantly, and the sight of a familiar person from that period can feel charged before they have even spoken. When she sits in an exam room for a routine medical visit, her body is so tense and expectant that the rustle of gloves or the opening of a tray can seem like confirmation that she is back in the same helpless, dangerous place.

Her job has made this especially hard to contain. As a network engineer she works in an environment built around sudden alerts, quick movement, and high-stakes problem solving. During incidents, people gather around screens, speak sharply, and move fast behind her chair. She has begun dreading those moments, not because she doubts her technical skill, but because the combination of raised voices and abrupt motion sends her into the same alarmed state. At home, she notices herself listening for changes in sound and checking on her son repeatedly even on quiet evenings. She knows he is currently safe, but she has come to believe that letting her guard down would be reckless, as though vigilance is the only thing standing between her family and another medical crisis. That constant readiness leaves her exhausted, and the exhaustion seems to make her even more reactive when reminders appear.

Moana finally sought help after nearly leaping out of her chair during a routine pediatric follow-up when a nurse moved suddenly at her son’s side. She was flooded with the old physical terror and could not stop trembling in the car afterward. What frightened her most was how small the trigger had become: not an emergency, just a familiar medical room and one quick movement. She worries that she is teaching her son that the world is unsafe and that she will never feel calm, even in her own home. At the same time, she is hopeful in a guarded way. She wants to be able to sit through an appointment, hear raised voices at work, or run into people from that time without her body reacting as if his life is in danger all over again.
